question_text: Match the following: (P) Condition coverage (Q) Equivalence class partitioning (R) Volume testing (S) Alpha testing (i) Black-box testing (ii) System testing (iii) White-box testing (iv) Performance testing
solution: Condition coverage is a white‑box testing technique (P‑iii). Equivalence partitioning is a black‑box testing method (Q‑i). Volume testing checks performance under large data volumes (R‑iv). Alpha testing is performed by developers before system release, a type of system testing (S‑ii).

question_text: Which one of the following is the recurrence equation for the worst case time complexity of the Quicksort algorithm for sorting n (≥2) numbers? (c is a constant)
solution: In worst case, Quicksort's pivot is the smallest/largest element, leading to one subproblem of size n‑1 and one of size 1. Partitioning takes O(n).

question_text: For any two languages L1 and L2 such that L1 is context‑free and L2 is recursively enumerable but not recursive, which of the following is/are necessarily true? I. complement(L1) is recursive II. complement(L2) is recursive III. complement(L1) is context‑free IV. complement(L1) ∪ L2 is recursively enumerable
solution: L1 is CFL, its complement is CSL hence recursive (I true). L2 is RE but not recursive, so its complement is not RE (II false). Complement of CFL is not necessarily CFL (III false). Union of CFL (or recursive) with RE is RE (IV true).

question_text: Evaluate lim x→∞ x^(1/x)
solution: Let y = x^(1/x) → ln y = (ln x)/x → limit 0. Hence y → e^0 = 1.

question_text: If g(x)=1-x and h(x)=x/(x-1), then g(h(x))/h(g(x)) is:
Match the following: (P) Prim's algorithm (Q) Floyd-Warshall algorithm (R) Mergesort (S) Hamiltonian circuit (i) Backtracking (ii) Greedy method (iii) Dynamic programming (iv) Divide and conquer
solution: Prim's uses greedy approach. Floyd‑Warshall uses dynamic programming. Merge sort is divide‑and‑conquer. Hamiltonian circuit is typically solved using backtracking.

question_text: SELECT operation in SQL is equivalent to
option_a: the selection operation in relational algebra
option_b: the selection operation in relational algebra, except that SELECT in SQL retains duplicates
option_c: the projection operation in relational algebra
option_d: the projection operation in relational algebra, except that SELECT in SQL retains duplicates
solution: SQL SELECT (without DISTINCT) does not eliminate duplicates by default, unlike relational algebra's projection (π) which returns a set (no duplicates).

question_text: For computers based on three‑address instruction formats, each address field can be used to specify which of the following: S1 A memory operand S2 A processor register S3 An implied accumulator register
option_d: All of S1, S2 and S3
solution: A three‑address instruction has explicit operand fields; they can refer to memory addresses or registers. An implied accumulator is not used in three‑address format.

question_text: The following two functions P1 and P2 share variable B=2 and execute concurrently. P1{ C = B-1; B = 2*C; } P2{ D = 2*B; D = D-1; } The number of distinct values that B can possibly take after execution is
solution: Possible values: (1) P1 then P2 → B=2; (2) P2 then P1 → B=3; (3) interleaved → e.g. P1 reads B=2, P2 reads B=2, then B can become 4. Distinct B values = 2,3,4.

question_text: Which of the following is/are correct inorder traversal sequence(s) of binary search tree(s)? I. 3,5,7,8,15,19,25 II. 5,8,9,12,10,15,25 III. 2,7,10,8,14,16,20 IV. 4,6,7,9,18,20,25
solution: Inorder of a BST must be strictly increasing (no duplicates). I and IV are strictly increasing. II has 12 then 10 (decrease). III has 10 then 8 (decrease).

question_text: void f1(int a, int b){ int c; c=a; a=b; b=c; } void f2(int *a, int *b){ int c; c=*a; *a=*b; *b=c; } int main(){ int a=4, b=5, c=6; f1(a,b); f2(&b,&c); printf("%d",c-a-b); } Output?
solution: f1 swaps local copies (no effect on main). f2 swaps values at b and c → b becomes 6, c becomes 5. Then c‑a‑b = 5‑4‑6 = -5.

question_text: Consider a system with byte‑addressable memory, 32‑bit logical addresses, 4 kilobyte page size and page table entries of 4 bytes each. The size of the page table in megabytes is
solution: Page size = 4KB = 2^12 bytes. Number of pages = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 pages. Page table size = 2^20 * 4 bytes = 4 MB.

question_text: Which one of the following is TRUE at any valid state in shift‑reduce parsing?
option_a: Viable prefixes appear only at the bottom of the stack
option_b: Viable prefixes appear only at the top of the stack
option_c: The stack contains only a set of viable prefixes
option_d: The stack never contains viable prefixes
solution: A viable prefix is a prefix of a right‑sentential form that can appear on the stack. During shift‑reduce parsing, the stack content is always a viable prefix, and it appears at the top.

question_text: Which one of the following is NOT equivalent to p ↔ q ?
solution: p ↔ q is true when p and q are identical. Option C is (p XOR q), which is the negation of equivalence.

question_text: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE? I. XML overcomes limitations in HTML for structured content. II. XML is not case sensitive while HTML is case sensitive. III. XML supports user defined tags; HTML uses pre‑defined tags. IV. XML tags need not be closed; HTML tags must be closed.
solution: XML is case sensitive; HTML is not (II false). XML tags must be closed (IV false). I and III are true.

question_text: For set A = {5,{6},{7}}, power set 2^A. Which are TRUE? I. ∅ ∈ 2^A II. ∅ ⊆ 2^A III. {5,{6}} ∈ 2^A IV. {5,{6}} ⊆ 2^A
solution: I true: empty set is element of power set. II true: empty set is subset of every set. III false: {5,{6}} is a subset of A, hence an element of 2^A (it is ∈). IV false: it is not a subset of 2^A.

question_text: In one pair below, both protocols can use multiple TCP connections between same client and server. Which one?
solution: HTTP (with persistent or parallel connections) can use multiple TCP connections. FTP uses separate control and data connections (multiple TCP). TELNET and SMTP typically use a single connection.

solution: I false: sequence number increments by segment data length (bytes). III false: advertised window changes with receiver buffer availability. II and IV are true.

question_text: 4‑bit Johnson counter with initial value 0000. Counting sequence is
solution: Johnson counter connects complement of last flip‑flop to first. 4‑bit sequence: 0000→1000→1100→1110→1111→0111→0011→0001→0000. In decimal: 0,8,12,14,15,7,3,1,0.

question_text: N people want pairwise secret communication using symmetric key cryptography. Number of keys required?
solution: Each pair needs a unique key. Number of pairs = C(N,2) = N(N‑1)/2.

question_text: Which IP header field is NOT modified by a typical IP router?
solution: Routers decrement TTL and update checksum. Length may change if fragmentation occurs. Source address remains unchanged.

question_text: Worst‑case complexities of insertion and deletion of a key in a binary search tree?
option_c: θ(n) for insertion, θ(log n) for deletion
option_d: θ(log n) for insertion, θ(n) for deletion
solution: In worst case (skewed tree), height = n. Insertion and deletion both require traversing from root to leaf → O(n).

question_text: A file is organized so that the ordering of data records is the same as or close to the ordering of data entries in some index. Then that index is called
solution: Clustered index determines the physical order of data records. (Spelling variant 'clustered' = 'clustered').

question_text: The height of a tree is the length of the longest root‑to‑leaf path. Maximum and minimum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 5 are
solution: Maximum nodes = 2^(5+1)-1 = 63 (full binary tree). Minimum nodes = 5+1 = 6 (a single chain of 6 nodes).

question_text: SQL query: SELECT S.Student Name, sum(P.Marks) FROM Student S, Performance P WHERE S.Roll No = P.Roll No GROUP BY S.Student Name. Number of rows returned?
solution: Two students share name 'Raj' (Roll 1 and 3). GROUP BY name combines them. Rohit is another group. Total 2 rows.

question_text: Binary operator ≠ defined by truth table (XOR). Which is true?
solution: XOR (exclusive OR) is both commutative (p⊕q = q⊕p) and associative ( (p⊕q)⊕r = p⊕(q⊕r) ).

question_text: Probability of no collision in first slot for stations with transmit probabilities 0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4.
Disk requests: 45,20,90,10,50,60,80,25,70. Initial head 50. Additional distance traversed by SSTF compared to SCAN (towards 100).
C function fun1: outer loop n times, inner loops. Return value approximates?
solution: Outer runs n times. First inner runs log₂n times (j=j/2). p ≈ log₂n. Second inner runs log₂p times ≈ log₂(log₂n). Total ≈ n log₂(log₂n).

question_text: Insert 35 into max heap 40,30,20,10,15,16,17,8,4. New heap?
solution: Insert 35 at end (index 10), then heapify up: swap with parent 15 (index 5) → 30 (index 2) → stop. Result matches option B.

question_text: Post condition for pseudo‑code (division algorithm) with x,y positive integers.
solution: The loop computes quotient q and remainder r such that x = q*y + r and 0 ≤ r < y.

question_text: Lattice L={p,q,r,s,t} with Hasse diagram. Probability that (x,y,z) in L^3 satisfies distributive law x∨(y∧z) = (x∨y)∧(x∨z).
solution: The given lattice is non‑distributive (pentagon). Out of 125 triples, 80 satisfy the equality, so pr = 80/125 = 0.64, which lies between 0.2 and 1.

question_text: C code: unsigned int x[4][3]={{...}}; address of x is 2000. printf("%u,%u,%u", x+3, *(x+3), *(x+2)+3);
solution: x+3 points to row 3: 2000 + 3*3*4 = 2036. *(x+3) is same address (type pointer to row). *(x+2)+3 points to row 2 element 3: 2000 + 2*3*4 + 3*4 = 2036. All three print 2036.

question_text: 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues -1 and 7. Find a and b.
solution: Trace = 1+b = -1+7 = 6 → b=5. Determinant = b - 4a = -7 → 5 - 4a = -7 → a=3.

question_text: D flip‑flop connected to JK flip‑flop. Initial D=1, JK=0. Sequence at JK Q output?
solution: The circuit forms a mod‑3 counter pattern. Initial states: D=1, JK=0. Next clock: JK Q becomes 1, D becomes 0. Sequence: 0,1,1,0,0,1,1,0,... matching option D.

question_text: Non‑pipelined: 2.5 GHz, CPI=4. Upgraded to 5‑stage pipeline, 2 GHz, no stalls. Speedup?
solution: Non‑pipelined time per instruction = 4 / 2.5 ns = 1.6 ns. Pipelined time = 1 / 2 ns = 0.5 ns. Speedup = 1.6 / 0.5 = 3.2.

question_text: Which of {f} or {g} is functionally complete? f = X'YZ + XY' + Y'Z' ; g = X'YZ + X'YZ' + XY
solution: f simplifies to X'Y + XY' + Y'Z' which can realize NAND/NOR, hence functionally complete. g simplifies to X'Y + XY = Y, not complete.

question_text: Data structure for operations: (log N)^1/2 find, N insert, (log N)^1/2 delete (with pointer), (log N)^1/2 decrease‑key. Best total asymptotic complexity?
solution: Min‑heap supports insert O(log N), decrease‑key O(log N), find O(1) for min but general find O(N). However N insert dominates, and heap gives O(N log N) overall best.

question_text: ER model: E1 and E2 m:n, E1 and E3 1:n (1 at E1). Minimum relations in 3NF.
solution: E1, E2, E3 each need a relation. m:n relationship R12 requires a separate relation. 1:n relationship R13 can be merged into E3. Total 4 relations.

question_text: Cyclomatic complexity of given C program segment.
solution: The code has 4 decision points: while(first<=last), if(array[middle]<search), else if(array[middle]==search), and if(first>last). CC = P + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.

question_text: Graph with 8 edges, MST weight 36 contains edges (A,C),(B,C),(B,E),(E,F),(D,F). Minimum sum of all 8 edges?
solution: To keep MST weight minimal, non‑MST edges must be just greater than the max edge on their cycle. Sum of given edges + min extra weights yields 69.

question_text: BFS tree T from source s. (u,v) edge of G not in T. Which d(u)-d(v) CANNOT be?
solution: In BFS tree, non‑tree edges connect nodes at same level or adjacent levels. So difference in distance can be -1, 0, or 1, but not 2 (or more).

question_text: Rate monotonic scheduling: T1(3,1), T2(7,2), T3(20,4). First instance of T3 completes at end of ___ ms.
solution: Priorities: T1 highest, then T2. Timeline: T1 runs at 0,3,6,9; T2 runs at 1,8; T3 runs remaining slots. First T3 instance finishes at time 12 ms.

question_text: Page references: 3,8,2,3,9,1,6,3,8,9,3,6,2,1,3 with 5 frames. FIFO vs LRU page faults?
solution: Both FIFO and LRU yield 9 page faults for this reference string with 5 frames.

question_text: Disk: seek 4ms, 10000 RPM, 600 sectors/track, 512 bytes/sector. Read 2000 sectors (each requires seek+rotational latency). Total time (ms)?
solution: Rotation time = 60/10000 = 6ms, avg latency = 3ms. Transfer per sector = 6/600 = 0.01ms. Time per sector = 4+3+0.01 = 7.01ms. Total = 2000 * 7.01 = 14020ms.

question_text: Recurrence for a_n: number of bit strings of length n with two consecutive 1s.
solution: Consider strings ending with 0 (a_{n-1}), ending with 01 (a_{n-2}), and ending with 11 (2^{n-2} possibilities for first n‑2 bits). Sum = a_{n-2}+a_{n-1}+2^{n-2}.

question_text: Live variable analysis at blocks 2 and 3 in CFG. Variables live at both?
solution: From the flow graph, variables r and u are live both at the statement in block 2 and block 3.

question_text: NPDA given. String that must follow 101100 for acceptance?

question_text: DFAs M and N given. Number of states in minimal DFA for L(M) ∩ L(N)
solution: M accepts strings with even number of 1's, N accepts odd number of 1's. Intersection is empty. Minimal DFA for empty language has 1 (non‑accepting) state.

question_text: Stop‑and‑wait: bit rate 64 kbps, propagation delay 20ms. Minimum frame size for 50% utilization?
solution: Utilization = 1/(1+2a) ≥ 0.5 → a ≤ 0.5. a = propagation delay / transmission time. Let t_trans = frame size / 64kbps. 20ms / t_trans ≤ 0.5 → t_trans ≥ 40ms. Frame size ≥ 64*10^3 * 40*10^-3 = 2560 bits = 320 bytes.

question_text: Connected planar graph with 10 vertices, each face has 3 edges. Number of edges?
Minimum temporary variables for three‑address SSA form of expression q + r/3 + s - t*5 + u*v/w
solution: Expression has 6 binary operations. SSA requires each temporary assigned once. Reusing temporaries optimally requires 5 temporary variables.

question_text: Consider the following two statements. S1: If a candidate is known to be corrupt, then he will not be elected. S2: If a candidate is kind, he will be elected. Which one follows from S1 and S2 as per sound inference rules?
option_a: If a person is known to be corrupt, he is kind
option_b: If a person is not known to be corrupt, he is not kind
option_c: If a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt
option_d: If a person is not kind, he is not known to be corrupt
solution: S1: Corrupt → ¬Elected. S2: Kind → Elected. Contrapositive of S2: ¬Elected → ¬Kind. Chaining: Corrupt → ¬Elected → ¬Kind, i.e., Corrupt → ¬Kind. Equivalent to Kind → ¬Corrupt.

question_text: The cardinality of the power set of {0,1,2,…,10} is
solution: Set has 11 elements. Power set size = 2^11 = 2048.

question_text: Let R be the relation on positive integers: aRb iff a and b are distinct and have a common divisor >1. Which is true?
option_a: R is symmetric and reflexive but not transitive
option_b: R is reflexive but not symmetric and not transitive
option_c: R is transitive but not reflexive and not symmetric
option_d: R is symmetric but not reflexive and not transitive
solution: Symmetric: if a,b share divisor, so do b,a. Not reflexive: requires distinct elements. Not transitive: e.g., (2,6) and (6,3) share divisors, but 2 and 3 are coprime.

question_text: An unordered list contains n distinct elements. Number of comparisons to find an element neither max nor min is
solution: Pick any three elements; the median of these three is neither overall max nor min. This takes constant comparisons.

question_text: Minimum number of JK flip-flops for synchronous counter with sequence (0,0,1,1,2,2,3,3,0,0,…) is
solution: Sequence has 8 distinct states before repeating (0,0,1,1,2,2,3,3). 2^3=8, so 3 flip‑flops needed.

question_text: Cache read: hit time 5ns, miss time 50ns. Hit rate 80%. Average read access time (ns) is
Computer: 40-bit virtual address, 8KB page, 128-entry TLB (32 sets, 4-way). TLB tag length (bits) is
solution: Page offset = 13 bits (8KB). Virtual page number = 40-13=27 bits. Set index = log2(32)=5 bits. Tag = 27-5=22 bits.

question_text: Which statements are true? I. Complement of every Turing decidable language is Turing decidable. II. There exists a language in NP but not Turing decidable. III. If L is in NP, L is Turing decidable.
solution: I true: decidable languages closed under complement. II false: NP ⊆ decidable. III true: NP implies decidable.

question_text: C function foo(char *a){ if(*a && *a!=' ') { foo(a+1); putchar(*a); } } on input "ABCD EFGH" outputs?
solution: Recursion prints characters after recursive call, reversing each word. For "ABCD", prints "DCBA". Stops at space.

question_text: Complete binary tree where left and right subtrees of root are max-heaps. Lower bound to convert to heap is
solution: Only root may violate heap property; one heapify-down takes O(log n) time.

question_text: Binary tree T has 20 leaves. Number of nodes with two children is
solution: In a binary tree, nodes with two children = leaves - 1 = 19.

solution: SRS describes what the system should do, not how (design).

question_text: Decision problems Q1 and Q2: Q1 ≤p 3-SAT and 3-SAT ≤p Q2. Which is consistent?
solution: Q1 reduces to 3-SAT (in NP) → Q1 ∈ NP. 3-SAT reduces to Q2 → Q2 is NP-hard.

question_text: Match: P.Lexical analysis Q.Parsing R.Register allocation S.Expression evaluation 1.Graph coloring 2.DFA minimization 3.Post-order traversal 4.Production tree
solution: Lexical → DFA minimization (2). Parsing → production tree (4). Register allocation → graph coloring (1). Expression evaluation → post-order (3).

question_text: AST vs CFG: Which is TRUE?
option_a: In both, successor node's code appears after predecessor's code
option_c: Max successors depend on input program
option_d: Each node corresponds to at most one statement
solution: AST nodes can have variable number of children; CFG nodes can have multiple outgoing edges depending on program structure.

question_text: Basic COCOMO equations form
solution: Basic COCOMO: Effort = a × (KLOC)^b, Development time = c × (Effort)^d.

question_text: System has 6 identical resources, N processes each can request at most 2. Which N could lead to deadlock?
solution: Maximum demand per process = 2. Deadlock possible if N*2 > 6 and resources held by all. For N=4, if each holds 1 and requests 1, deadlock.

question_text: Transaction: read(x); x:=x-50; write(x); read(y); y:=y+50; write(y). Constraint sum constant is
solution: The sum remaining constant is a consistency requirement (invariant).

question_text: B+ tree index of order 1 shown. Minimum nodes fetched for query "key ≥7 and <15" is
solution: Traverse root to leaf for 7, then follow sibling pointers. Count includes root, internal node, and leaf nodes accessed.

question_text: Correct order of socket API calls for server: accept, bind, listen, recv
solution: Server: bind → listen → accept → recv.

question_text: Link speed 10^6 bps, packet 1000 bytes, stop-and-wait efficiency 25%. One-way propagation delay (ms) is
solution: Efficiency = 1/(1+2a) = 0.25 → a=1.5. Transmission time = 8000 bits / 10^6 = 8 ms. a = propagation/transmission → propagation = 12 ms.

question_text: Which is NOT correct about HTTP cookies?
option_a: Cookie is a piece of code compromising security
option_b: Cookie gains entry via HTTP header
solution: Cookies are data, not executable code. They do not compromise security by themselves.

question_text: UDP datagram 8880 bytes user data over Ethernet (MTU 1500). IP header 20, UDP header 8. Number of fragments and last fragment offset?
solution: Total IP datagram = 8880+8=8888 bytes. Max payload per fragment = 1500-20=1480, must be multiple of 8. 8888/1480 = 6 fragments + remainder. Need 7 fragments. Last offset = (1480*6)/8 = 1110.

question_text: TCP bandwidth 1048560 bps. α: RTT after which window scale needed; β: max window with scale. α and β are
solution: Window size field 16 bits → max 65535 bytes. Bandwidth×RTT = 65535 → RTT ≈ 500ms. Scale factor up to 14 (max window 65535×2^14).

question_text: Checkpointing log recovery: undo and redo lists after crash
solution: After checkpoint, T2 committed → redo. T1 and T3 not committed → undo. T4 committed before checkpoint → nothing.

question_text: R1(A,B)={(1,5),(3,7)} R2(A,C)={(1,7),(4,9)}. Full natural outer join R contains?
solution: Natural join on A: matches A=1 gives (1,5,7). Left outer adds (3,7,null) and right outer adds (4,null,9). question_text: Memory partitions 200,400,600,500,300,250 KB. Processes 357,210,468,491 KB. Best fit allocation leaves which partitions unused?
Disk: 15000 RPM, transfer 50×10^6 B/s, seek = 2×rotational delay, controller transfer = 10×disk transfer. Average time for 512B sector (ms)
solution: Rotational delay = 0.5×(60/15000)=2ms. Seek = 4ms. Disk transfer = 512/(50×10^6) ≈ 0.01024ms. Controller transfer = 0.1024ms. Total ≈ 4+2+0.01024+0.1024 = 6.11ms.

question_text: System: 8KB pages, 32-bit physical address. Page table entry includes valid, dirty, 3 permission bits, translation. Max page table size 24MB. Virtual address length (bits)
solution: Physical pages = 2^32/2^13 = 2^19 frames. Page table entry size ≈ 4 bytes? Actually 24MB/8KB = 3072 entries per process? question_text: Intermediate code control-flow graph: number of nodes and edges
solution: Basic blocks: B1(1-2), B2(3-9), B3(10-11). Edges: B1→B2, B2→B2 (loop), B2→B3, B3→B2 (outer loop). Total 6 nodes, 7 edges.

question_text: Minimum DFA states for regular expression (0+1)*(10)
solution: Language: strings ending with 10. DFA needs states: start, after 1, after 10 (final). Total 3 states.

solution: Dijkstra → greedy (iii). Floyd‑Warshall → DP (ii). Binary search → divide & conquer (i). Backtracking → depth‑first search (iv).

question_text: Graph G from K_{3,4} by adding vertex s adjacent to all vertices. Minimum edge-colouring colours
solution: Maximum degree Δ = max(3+1,4+1) = 5? Actually s connects to 7 vertices, degree 7. So Δ=7. By Vizing's theorem, edge-chromatic number = Δ or Δ+1. Bipartite K_{3,4} has edge-chromatic 4, adding s increases max degree to 7. Need 7 colors.

question_text: Paging: TLB hit 95%, page fault 10%. Mem access 100ns, TLB 20ns, disk transfer 5000ns. 20% faults dirty page write back. Avg memory access time (ns, 1 decimal)
solution: Effective access time = 0.95*(20+100) + 0.05*[0.9*(20+100+100) + 0.1*5000]? Actually with page fault: TLB hit then page fault possible. Compute: TLB hit (95%) → mem access (100ns) if no PF, else disk. TLB miss (5%) → mem access for page table (100ns) then same. Overall AMAT ≈ 154.8ns.

question_text: B+ tree: block 4KB, key 12B, pointer 8B, 1 million records, each record one block. Minimum disk accesses to retrieve any record
solution: Order of internal node: n*8 + (n-1)*12 ≤ 4096 → n ≈ 204. With 1M records, leaf nodes = 1M/(records per leaf). Height = ceil(log_{204}(1M)) + 1 = 2+1=3? Plus root access = 4 total.

question_text: TCP: RTT 6ms, window 50KB, threshold 32KB, MSS 2KB. Congestion window size at t+60ms after all ACKs (KB)
solution: Slow start: each RTT doubles cwnd. Start 2KB. RTT=6ms, 60ms = 10 RTT. cwnd doubles until threshold 32KB, then linear increase. At 60ms, cwnd = 44KB.
